dedupe_keys.name: hesketh out marsh saltmarsh recreation by managed realignment ribble estuary

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes Hesketh Out Marsh on the southern shore of the Ribble estuary near Preston, UK, one of the largest managed realignment projects in the country. The saltmarsh had been cut off from the estuary by an outer wall in 1980 and farmed; with sea levels rising, the RSPB and the Environment Agency strengthened an inland bank and let seawater back in through breaches, re-creating saltmarsh that stores floodwater, dissipates waves and provides important bird habitat. Work began in 2006 with land purchase, the first phase finished in 2008, and the final breach of the outer bank in 2017 completed the second phase, whose out-turn cost was 7.2 million pounds; using local soil for the bank saved about 2 million pounds. Partners included the Environment Agency, RSPB, Natural England and Lancaster City Council. The page, published in 2016 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal with a link to the RSPB reserve page. Caveats: first-phase costs are not available, and concerns of local stakeholders had to be addressed. It illustrates nature-based coastal flood hazard reduction and climate adaptation of estuary defences; related records are the Kruibeke Bazel Rupelmonde and Sand Motor case studies and WDPA.
name: Hesketh Out Marsh saltmarsh recreation by managed realignment (Ribble estuary)
organisations: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds
outcomes: Saltmarsh was re-created behind a stronger inland bank in two phases completed in 2008 and 2017, improving flood defence and creating a major estuarine bird habitat.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study from the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB)
